# Three questions, not one

A model that outputs a probability is asked to do three different jobs, and it
can do any one of them well while failing the others. "Is it a good model?" is
really three questions wearing one coat [@steyerberg2010].

## 1. Discrimination — can it rank?

Given an event and a non-event, does the model score the event higher? This is
ranking, and nothing else. It asks whether the model puts patients in the right
*order*, and it is completely indifferent to what the numbers on that order
actually are. A model whose every probability is divided by ten discriminates
exactly as well as before.

AUROC measures this, and only this. Chapter 4 builds it. Its blind spot is
everything to do with the numbers themselves, which is the whole of the next
question.

## 2. Calibration — do the numbers mean what they say?

When the model says 0.8, does the event happen about 80% of the time? A model
can rank perfectly and still be badly calibrated — confident when it should be
cautious, or the reverse — and you cannot tell from the AUROC, because ranking
survives any monotone rescaling of the score.

Calibration is the question that matters the moment a probability is read as a
probability: fed to a threshold, shown to a clinician, multiplied into an
expected cost. It is also, reliably, the first thing to break when a model
trained in one population meets another, and the last thing anyone reports
[@vancalster2019]. Chapter 6 builds two ways to measure it, and shows them
disagreeing.

## 3. Utility — is it worth using here?

Even a well-ranked, well-calibrated model has to earn its place against the
decision it informs. Acting on a prediction has costs — a false alarm is not
free, and neither is a missed case — and those costs are not symmetric and not
the same in every setting. Decision-analytic tools such as net benefit weigh
them explicitly [@vickers2006].

This book concentrates on the first two questions, where most evaluation
mistakes are made, and treats utility through its most common proxy: the
operating threshold. Chapter 7 shows that a single fixed threshold — "refer if
p > 0.7" — is itself a utility judgement, and one that quietly costs different
groups very different amounts.

## Why the separation matters

Keeping the three apart is not pedantry; it is what lets you locate a failure.

| A model can be… | …while being… | Symptom |
|---|---|---|
| well-ranked | miscalibrated | AUROC fine, probabilities untrustworthy |
| calibrated on average | miscalibrated per subgroup | pooled numbers reassuring, group numbers not |
| ranked and calibrated | wrong for this decision | good metrics, poor net benefit at the used threshold |

Every chapter that follows is an instance of this table. The tools differ; the
lesson does not: a single number answers a single question, and there are three.

With the questions named, we need somewhere to answer them where we already
know the answer. That is the simulator.
